title: Schizophrenic lunged at officers with knife, inquest told
article: Grinding his teeth and breathing heavily, his body in a fighting stance, Byron Debassige lunged at two police officers with a pocket knife, prompting them to shoot from just a few feet away, a coroner's inquest into the 28-year-old's death heard Tuesday.

Both officers testified that they couldn't back down, as Mr. Debassige was a danger to the public, that they couldn't shoot him in the arm as they might have missed. They also said that the schizophrenic man's mental illness was irrelevant to how they dealt with him on a cold winter evening in February 2008.

Constable John Tanner told the inquest he and partner Constable Bradley Coutts were returning to the station from an assignment around 8:20 p.m. that night when they heard an urgent call over their two-way radio: A man had lifted some lemons from a fruit store, threatened clerks with a knife and fled towards the Davisville subway.
As they drove down nearby Chaplin Crescent, the officers saw a man matching Mr. Debassige's description heading into Oriole Park and walked into the park to head him off.

Constable Coutts testified Mr. Debassige was walking unsteadily, singing and carrying a liquor bottle. When they told him to put it down, he pulled the knife out of his pocket, flicked it open and mumbled something.

"It was something along the lines of 'you're getting some,' " Constable Tanner testified, adding the officers drew their guns and backed away, shouting at Mr. Debassige to drop the knife and threatening to shoot. For a moment, he paused.

Standing up on the witness stand, the officer demonstrated how Mr. Debassige positioned his body - dropping his shoulders, leaning forward and holding the knife in front of him - which Constable Tanner described as a fighting stance.

"The male started grinding his teeth, heavy breathing, lowered his centre of gravity and lunged towards me," he said. Both officers fired. For a moment, Mr. Debassige stared at them, then grabbed his stomach and toppled to the ground, they said. He was pronounced dead within the hour.

During cross-examination, Debassige family lawyer Barry Swadron pointed out the police officers hadn't attempted to talk the young man down and that, while officers are trained in such techniques by fellow police, they have no instruction from psychiatrists, psychologists or social workers. "They don't have the training to deal with people with mental illness and it's about time they did," he told reporters during a break in the proceedings. "[Constable Tanner]followed his training and we have a dead man."

Robert Baldwin, lawyer for the Police Services Board said the force was open to improvements if the inquest suggests some. "If the evidence discloses that changes should be made in training...the chief would certainly consider it," he said outside court.
For their part, the officers insisted that, had they known of Mr. Debassige's illness, it wouldn't have changed their course of action.

"I think if we had done anything differently in the same circumstances, one of us could be maimed or dead," said Constable Coutts, who was himself taken to hospital that night to be treated for stress.
Such assertions were of no comfort to Mr. Debassige's half-sister, Angie Assinewe, who observed the proceedings for a second day.

"I'm glad that we're able to see the person face to face - I was dreading putting a face to the people who killed my brother," she said. "The policeman's comment that he would do it again was upsetting."
The inquest continues.

By the time a knife-wielding Byron Debassige was shot dead by police in a Toronto park on a winter evening, he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia, battled alcoholism and been assigned case workers to help him deal with his mental illness.

How social agencies, health-care workers and the officers themselves dealt with the 28-year-old - and, by extension, how they must deal with mentally ill people in violent situations in the future - will be the central issues at a coroner's inquiry that began Monday.

In her opening address to the jury, the coroner's lawyer framed the quasi-judicial proceeding as a chance to scrutinize the services, including mental-health case workers and a group home, that tried to help the Ojibwa man in the months before his death.

"We will examine a little more of those supports to see if there is an opportunity to improve those services so others may benefit," she said. "It seemed Mr. Debassige could take advantage of the supports, but eventually his condition deteriorated."
The barrister for Mr. Debassige's family, however, set his sights squarely on police treatment of the mentally ill.
"There are a lot of people who deal with the same thing - security guards, health-care workers - who are threatened with knives, and they don't have guns," Barry Swadron said outside court.

Two years ago, the Special Investigations Unit cleared the officers involved, Constables John Tanner and Bradley Coutts, of wrongdoing in the Feb. 16, 2008, shooting, finding they had reason to believe their lives were in danger. During a recess, Joseph Markson, who is representing them at the inquiry, made a similar argument.
"When someone is coming at you with a knife, you must live or die in that moment," he said. "[Mr. Debassige's]mental health and intoxication is no longer of relevance to you at that point in time."

Yong Jian Su, whose sister owns a food store at Yonge Street and Davisville Avenue, testified that Mr. Debassige walked into the store around 8 p.m. and stole some lemons. When he confronted Mr. Debassige outside, he said, the young man first raised a juice bottle over his head, then pulled out a knife with a three-inch-long blade and made stabbing motions in the air. Mr. Su backed down and his sister called 911, he said, as Mr. Debassige walked away.
"He said, 'If you call the police, I will come back and get you,' " Mr. Su told the inquest.
Police tracked Mr. Debassige down at nearby Oriole Park, where they shot him.

Forensic toxicologist Marie Elliot told the jury Mr. Debassige had a blood alcohol level equivalent to more than 10 drinks at the time he was killed, along with traces of cannabis and prescription antidepressants in his blood.

John Doucet, who performed a postmortem on him, described how bullets had punctured the young man's lung, liver and kidney. As Dr. Doucet explained the injuries, Mr. Debassige's half-sister, Angie Assinewe, sat in the front row of the public gallery, wiping away tears.
"It's our hope the coroner's inquest can help us answer some of the questions surrounding Byron's death," she said outside. "We're sorry this day ever had to come."
The inquest can make recommendations to prevent similar deaths in future, but cannot assign criminal responsibility in the case.
An inquest will probe the death of a man shot and killed by police in a Toronto park more than two years ago, the office of the coroner announced Tuesday.
Bryan DeBassige, 28, was shot on February 28, 2008 in Oriole Park, near Yonge Street and Davisville Avenue and died later in hospital.

A 2008 probe by the Special Investigations Unit determined that Mr. DeBassige had stolen lemons from a nearby convenience store and pulled a knife on the owners. When police confronted him, he brandished the three-inch knife in a "threatening" pose and walked towards them, ignoring their instructions to drop the weapon, the SIU concluded. Investigators decided not to lay charges against the officers.

"The evidence establishes that each officer shot Mr. DeBassige believing it necessary to protect himself and his partner from death or grievous bodily harm," wrote SIU director James Cornish at the time.
Mr. DeBassige's family, however, said he had a lengthy history of mental illness and argued the police should have done more to talk him down.
The Coroner's Inquest can't assign blame in the case, but can determine the circumstances of Mr. DeBassige's death and make recommendations to prevent similar deaths in the future.
The inquest begins Monday of next week in Toronto. It is scheduled to last 10 days and will hear evidence from about 20 witnesses.

The inquest comes less than a month after Reyal Jensen Jardine-Douglas, a 25-year-old man who family said suffered from paranoia, was shot dead following an altercation with police after he stepped off a Scarborough bus.

A 2007 inquest into the death of O'Brien-Christopher Reid, a mentally ill man shot dead by police when he lunged at them with a knife in a Toronto park in June 2004, recommended that police should be better trained to deal with people suffering from mental health issues.
